title: Imports: Real Analysis and Finite Sets
content: Imports Mathlib modules for natural numbers, real numbers, finite sets, and tactics. These provide the foundation for defining ℝ² points, distance functions, and finite point configurations.
mathContext: The formalization uses $\mathbb{R}$ from `Data.Real.Basic` and `Finset` from `Data.Finset.Basic` to model finite point sets in the plane.

title: Point in ℝ²
content: Defines **Point2** as ℝ × ℝ, a point in the Euclidean plane. This is the ambient space for the distinct distances problem.
mathContext: A point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$ is represented as a pair $(p_1, p_2) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$.

title: Squared Euclidean Distance
content: Defines **distSq(p, q)** = (p₁ - q₁)² + (p₂ - q₂)², the squared Euclidean distance. Using squared distance avoids irrational numbers while preserving the distinct distances count.
mathContext: The squared distance $d^2(p,q) = (p_1 - q_1)^2 + (p_2 - q_2)^2$ is a standard trick in discrete geometry: $d^2$ determines $d$ uniquely (for $d \ge 0$), so counting distinct $d^2$ values equals counting distinct distances.

title: Bipartite Distance Set
content: Defines **bipartiteDistSet(X, Y)** as the image of X ×ˢ Y under distSq. This is the set of all distinct squared distances between points in X and points in Y — the key object of study.
mathContext: The bipartite distance set $\Delta(X,Y) = \{d^2(x,y) \mid x \in X, y \in Y\}$ restricts to cross-distances only. Its cardinality $|\Delta(X,Y)|$ is the quantity $F(2n)$ minimizes over.

title: Extremal Function F(2n)
content: Axiomatizes **minBipartiteDist** representing F(2n), the minimum number of distinct bipartite distances achievable between two n-point sets in ℝ². Currently set to 0 as a placeholder — the true value is unknown.
mathContext: $F(2n) = \min_{|X|=|Y|=n} |\Delta(X,Y)|$ where the minimum is over all $n$-element point sets $X, Y \subset \mathbb{R}^2$. The problem asks for the growth rate of $F(2n)$.

title: Extremal Function f(2n)
content: Axiomatizes **minDistinct2n** representing f(2n), the minimum number of distinct distances among 2n general points in ℝ². Guth–Katz showed f(2n) = Θ(n/log n) up to a √(log n) factor.
mathContext: $f(2n) = \min_{|P|=2n} |\{d(p,q) \mid p,q \in P, p \ne q\}|$ where $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$. The Guth–Katz bound gives $\Omega(n/\log n) \le f(2n) \le O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$.

title: Erdős Problem #661: Bipartite Advantage Conjecture
content: **Main Conjecture**: For all ε > 0, there exists N₀ such that F(2n) ≤ ε · f(2n) for all n ≥ N₀. This is the formal statement that F(2n) = o(f(2n)) — the bipartite arrangement provides asymptotically fewer distinct distances.
mathContext: The axiom formalizes $F(2n) = o(f(2n))$ via the $\varepsilon$-$N_0$ definition of little-$o$: $\forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists N_0, \forall n \ge N_0: F(2n) \le \varepsilon \cdot f(2n)$. This is **OPEN** — neither proved nor disproved.

title: Guth–Katz Lower Bound (2015)
content: **Guth–Katz**: There exists C > 0 such that f(2n) ≥ C · n/log n for all n ≥ 2. This landmark result essentially resolved Erdős's original distinct distances problem (Problem #89) and establishes the baseline for the bipartite variant.
mathContext: Guth and Katz proved $f(n) = \Omega(n/\log n)$ using the Elekes–Sharir–Guth–Katz framework: (1) reduce to counting rich lines in $\mathbb{R}^3$, (2) map to the Lie group $SE(2)$ of rigid motions, (3) apply algebraic geometry of ruled surfaces to bound the number of lines on degree-2 surfaces. This was a major breakthrough in combinatorial geometry.

title: Lattice Upper Bound
content: **Integer Lattice Bound**: There exists C > 0 such that f(2n) ≤ C · n/√(log n) for all n ≥ 2. This is achieved by the grid {1,...,√n}² and follows from Landau's estimate on numbers representable as sums of two squares.
mathContext: The $\sqrt{n} \times \sqrt{n}$ integer lattice has $n$ points and $O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ distinct distances, by Landau's theorem: the number of integers $\le N$ that are sums of two squares is $\Theta(N/\sqrt{\log N})$. This gives the best known upper bound on $f(2n)$.

title: Lenz Construction in ℝ⁴
content: **Lenz's Construction**: In ℝ⁴, place n points on one unit circle and n points on a second unit circle in an orthogonal 2-plane. Then every bipartite distance equals √2, giving F(2n) = 1. This shows the problem is dimension-sensitive.
mathContext: Let $C_1 \subset \mathbb{R}^4$ be the unit circle in the $(x_1,x_2)$-plane and $C_2$ the unit circle in the $(x_3,x_4)$-plane. For $p \in C_1$ and $q \in C_2$: $d^2(p,q) = |p|^2 + |q|^2 = 1 + 1 = 2$, so $d(p,q) = \sqrt{2}$ for all pairs. This is impossible in $\mathbb{R}^2$ by Elekes–Rónyai type results.

title: Connection to Erdős Problem #89
content: Erdős Problem #89 is the general distinct distances problem: what is the minimum number of distinct distances among n points in ℝ²? Problem #661 is the bipartite variant. The general problem was essentially resolved by Guth–Katz; the bipartite version remains open.
mathContext: Problem #89 asks for $f(n)$; Problem #661 asks whether $F(2n) = o(f(2n))$. Since $F(2n) \le f(2n)$ trivially (any bipartite configuration is a special case of a general one), the question is whether strict inequality holds asymptotically.

title: $50 Reward
content: Erdős offered $50 for resolving whether F(2n) = o(f(2n)) in the plane. This moderate prize reflects the problem's difficulty but narrower scope compared to the $500 original distinct distances problem.
mathContext: Erdős's prize system ranged from \$25 (approachable) to \$10,000 (the twin prime conjecture). A \$50 prize indicates a problem Erdős considered tractable but non-trivial.
